study.title: Joshua 16 The inheritance of Ephraim and the permanence of the Canaanites in Gezer
study.overview: Joshua 16 describes the inheritance received by the sons of Joseph, with special attention to the territory of Ephraim. The chapter shows that the distribution of the land was not random: it fits into the promise given to Joseph's lineage and places these tribes in a central position in Canaan. At the same time, the text ends with an important tension: the Canaanites of Gezer were not expelled, but continued among the Ephraimites, although subject to tribute. Thus, the chapter combines fulfilled promise, definite boundaries and incomplete obedience.

outline.title: The inheritance of the sons of Joseph
outline.explanation: The initial verses summarize the portion given to Ephraim and Manasseh, sons of Joseph. The land extends from east to west, from the Jordan to the sea, indicating a wide and strategic distribution. The text highlights that the two branches of Joseph's family receive their inheritance together, fulfilling the blessing linked to Joseph and his posterity.

outline.title: The limits of Ephraim and the cities in their midst
outline.explanation: Here the focus goes to the specific territory of Ephraim. The chapter lists borders and places that delimit the inheritance, although the description is brief and, at some points, difficult to reconstruct accurately. It is also observed that there were cities of Ephraim inserted in the territory inherited amid the Manasseh area, showing a territorial coexistence among the sister tribes.

outline.title: Gezer and the Permanence of the Canaanites
outline.explanation: The chapter concludes with a note of partial infidelity: the Canaanites who lived in Gezer were not expelled. Instead, they remained among the Ephraimites, even though they were taxpayers. The verse makes it clear that the possession of the earth did not fully eliminate the Canaanite presence, revealing an incomplete conquest.

study.context: The chapter is part of the division of the promised land among the tribes of Israel. The text shows the sons of Joseph Ephraim and Manasseh - receiving central and valuable portions in the land of Canaan. The notes highlight that this distribution relates to the blessing pronounced on Joseph and the leadership position that his tribes would exercise. There is also reference to places such as Jericho, Bethel, Bete-Horom and Gezer, without the chapter explaining in detail each locality.
study.theology: Theologically, the chapter emphasizes that God's promise advances through the concrete distribution of the earth. The inheritance is not abstract: it translates into territory, borders and historical responsibility. At the same time, the permanence of the Canaanites in Gezer points to an incomplete obedience of Israel. Even receiving the inheritance, the people still live with resistance, which suggests that the possession of the promise does not automatically eliminate the call to full fidelity. The centrality of Ephraim also anticipates its importance within Israel, although the text does not turn this into automatic spiritual superiority.

scholarViews.insight: The tribes of Joseph, Ephraim, and the rest of Manasseh, receive their inheritance and this completes the total number of portions, in connection with Jacob's blessing on Joseph.
Joseph's portion is in the heart of Canaan, stretching from the Jordan to the sea, showing a central and favorable heritage, in harmony with the blessings received.
The Canaanites of Gezer were not expelled in fact, but the Ephraimites managed to submit them to tribute, without fully removing them from the land.

questions: What does the shape of the inheritance of Ephraim and Manasseh teach about God's faithfulness to his promises?
Why is the permanence of the Canaanites in Gezer theologically important to understand the incomplete obedience of Israel?
How can the central location of Joseph's inheritance have influenced the role of these tribes in the history of Israel?
study.practice: This chapter invites the reader to examine whether he has received God's promise with gratitude and also with practical obedience. Concrete application is twofold: to recognize that God fulfills what he promises and, at the same time, not to accept concessions that leave "the residual" occupying space that should be subjected to the Lord. In personal terms, this means dealing with areas of partial commitment to repentance and discipline, rather than normalizing them. In community terms, he calls the church to occupy its place without abandoning total fidelity to the will of God.
study.uncertainty: The description of the borders is brief and difficult to reconstruct accurately, and the notes recognize this limitation. Nor is it possible to safely affirm, only by this chapter, the precise correspondence of all the places mentioned with the modern geographical tracings. The notes provided do not allow to develop the historical context more than the text already suggests.
